title: Gibraltar's Chief Minister: Why This EU Treaty Works (And Where It Doesn't)
label: 15 September 2026 · Gibraltar treaty evidence
summary: Fabian Picardo, Gibraltar's Chief Minister, tells the House of Lords European Affairs Committee why 96% of Gibraltarians voted for this UK-EU treaty. He explains how it keeps the border with Spain flowing smoothly, why the European Court of Justice is only there to interpret shared rules, how people who are refused entry are handled, what the financial mechanism costs, and why Gibraltar can still do its own services trade deals. He admits the treaty is imperfect but says it protects sovereignty and keeps Gibraltar's economy going.

chapters.title: Why Gibraltar Voted 96% For This Treaty
chapters.takeaway: Brexit threatened to choke the daily flow of people and goods across Gibraltar's border, so an overwhelming majority backed a deal to keep things moving.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Welcome, Chief Minister. Why did 96% of Gibraltarians vote for this treaty? And how did people react to the UK's 2016 vote to leave the EU?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: 2016 was very difficult for us. Leaving the EU threatened to upend our economy and our daily lives. Thousands of people cross from Spain into Gibraltar every day for work or to see family, and new EU border rules would have made that much harder. People understood that without needing it explained.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you — that sets the scene. Baroness Suttie?

turns.speaker: Baroness Suttie
turns.text: What were the hardest practical problems Brexit caused, and will this agreement fix them?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: The biggest was fluidity at the border. Around 15,000 cross-border workers come in daily, mostly between 7am and 10am. Checking each person for 15 to 30 seconds with only two or three lanes would have caused massive queues. Those workers keep our public services — looking after our elderly, sick and children — and our online gaming and insurance industries running. Without them, we couldn't offer the high-standard services we do or raise the taxes that pay for them.

chapters.title: Did a Change of Government in the UK Speed Things Up?
chapters.takeaway: Both UK parties supported Gibraltar equally, but it was actually global security worries about Trump and Vance that gave the negotiations their biggest push.

turns.speaker: The Duke of Wellington
turns.text: When the UK government changed in 2024, did that affect the tone or speed of negotiations?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: Both UK parties have been equally supportive throughout. Negotiations started under a Conservative government, and I accompanied Lord Cameron to Brussels twice, and later David Lammy and Stephen Doughty. We thought a Labour government in the UK might move faster with a socialist government in Madrid, but honestly the biggest boost came from President Trump and Vice-President Vance's speech at the Munich Security Conference in February 2025. That made everyone realise the UK and Europe needed to work together, not fight over two and a half square miles of land.

chapters.title: Sovereignty and the European Court of Justice
chapters.takeaway: Gibraltar's British sovereignty is completely untouched, and the European Court of Justice is only there to make sure the same rules mean the same thing everywhere.

turns.speaker: Baroness Smith of Newnham
turns.text: Have the principles you and Dominic Raab set out in March 2021 been kept, especially the promise that sovereignty over Gibraltar would never pass to another state without your consent?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: Those weren't his aims; they were my aims and my negotiating team's aims, which the UK agreed to. That's what we call the double lock on Gibraltar's constitution, dating from 2006. It's a red line for any Gibraltar government. Not one iota of our sovereignty has been compromised. I can put my hand in the Gibraltarian political fire on that.

turns.speaker: Baroness Smith of Newnham
turns.text: I'm a Liberal Democrat, and my party has been very supportive of Gibraltar. I have no further questions.

turns.speaker: Lord Jackson of Peterborough
turns.text: The European Court of Justice will interpret EU rules under this treaty. Doesn't that infringe Gibraltar's sovereignty?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: Absolutely not. Gibraltar voted 96% to stay in the EU, which meant accepting the European Court of Justice's full jurisdiction. This is like agreeing to abide by the rules of a club and letting the club's dispute mechanism decide what those rules mean. If the same EU rule applies both in the EU and in our treaty, it can't be interpreted differently in each place. That's not sovereignty; it's just legal consistency.

chapters.title: Who Gets In and Who Gets Turned Away
chapters.takeaway: Gibraltar decides who can enter, and the Schengen area decides separately who can enter Spain and the rest of Europe; if one says no but the other says yes, the person can only go where they're allowed.

turns.speaker: Lord Brennan of Canton
turns.text: How does the agreement handle refusing someone entry? Who makes the final decision, and when? The earlier witnesses seemed a bit confused.

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: It's complex but workable. Gibraltar continues to make its own immigration decision — we accept or deny entry just as we do today. The Schengen area, which covers Spain and most of Europe, makes its own decision separately. If we let someone in but Schengen refuses them, they can visit Gibraltar only, not Spain. If we refuse them but Schengen lets them in, they can go through a separate exit at the airport and enter Spain and the rest of Schengen — just as if they'd landed in Cádiz or Málaga. We'd put their face in our recognition system so they know they can't enter Gibraltar.

turns.speaker: Lord Brennan of Canton
turns.text: So it's exit but not via the gift shop — you can't just wander through Gibraltar.

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: Exactly. And if we let someone in but they then cross into Spain without Schengen permission, they'd be in Spain illegally. It's like Germany letting you in but you having no Schengen visa, so you can't legally go to France. So far, in the two months we've been operating this, we've had no such cases — only people refused by both sides.

chapters.title: Tax, Money and Who Pays
chapters.takeaway: Gibraltar already meets top international tax standards and will pay for a training fund itself, not with UK taxpayers' money.

turns.speaker: Lord Grantchester
turns.text: The treaty commits you to good tax governance — transparency, information exchange and fair tax competition. How will that work?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: Gibraltar already meets all those standards. We were the first place in the EU — ahead of the UK, Germany and France — to have an open register showing who really owns companies. We're happy to sign up. It doesn't stop us being a competitive, well-regulated financial centre.

turns.speaker: Lord Elliott of Mickle Fell
turns.text: The treaty mentions a financial mechanism to promote regional cohesion. How much will Gibraltar pay, and will the UK contribute?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: Gibraltar will pay, not the UK taxpayer. We'll raise the money from our own taxpayers and some companies. It'll only be used to train people for the Gibraltar job market. It'll start in the low millions and may grow. When I became Chief Minister, we had about 6,000 to 7,000 cross-border workers; that's now around 15,500, and the economy has grown a lot.

chapters.title: What Happens Next and How It's Working
chapters.takeaway: The treaty is already being applied on a provisional basis to keep the border flowing, and while there have been teething problems, traffic and trade are recovering.

turns.speaker: Lord Barrow
turns.text: The Gibraltar Parliament unanimously endorsed the treaty in March. What was welcomed, and were there any concerns? And how does the concordat with the UK protect Gibraltar?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: The Parliament Hansard shows the debate. This is a compromise — I've called it imperfect but exactly what we need to keep going with our sovereignty intact. The concordat, like the one for the withdrawal agreement, sets out who does what and who pays for what. The UK has the international legal obligations, but Gibraltar does the work at the border and in our courts. The concordat has been scrutinised and found satisfactory.

turns.speaker: Baroness Ashton of Upholland
turns.text: The treaty has been provisionally applied since 15 July. Why not fully applied yet, and have any problems emerged?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: We had to avoid new EU biometric border checks — the Entry/Exit System — causing huge tailbacks. We couldn't ratify in time, so we included a provisional application clause. That let us keep people moving from 15 July, with full ratification expected in December. At the airport, when several planes land at once, there are some delays, but we're adding more booths. On customs, we had traffic issues early on — a local fair blocked lorry routes — and we need consistent procedures. Truck traffic dropped from 250–300 a day to 100–150, but it's back to normal now. The working groups are being set up to fix the sticky bits.

turns.speaker: Lord Jackson of Peterborough
turns.text: Have you published guidance on the new residency rules?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: Yes, we have. I can't recall the exact date, but I'll write to you with it.

chapters.title: Trade, Services and the Future
chapters.takeaway: Gibraltar can still make its own services trade deals, but it accepts some limits on goods in exchange for keeping the border open.

turns.speaker: Lord Tugendhat
turns.text: In the past, many British people on the Costa del Sol used Gibraltar banks for mortgages and pensions. Is that still true, and does the treaty help them?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: That's no longer a big part of our business. Most banks here don't offer services to non-residents now. British people in Spain mostly bank in Spain or the UK. Visitors come to shop or see Gibraltar, but they don't bank here. The treaty helps by keeping the border fluid for them.

turns.speaker: Lord Tugendhat
turns.text: Does this agreement settle things for the foreseeable future, or will more deals be needed?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: On fluidity, it's settled. I can't promise it'll never be relitigated — especially in a Spanish election year — but everyone seems happy with the current arrangements. Sovereignty is unchanged: the UK and Spain have both reserved their positions. Gibraltar still fights for self-determination at the UN, where we're on the list of non-self-governing territories. We've sorted Brussels, but we still have work to do in New York.

turns.speaker: Lord Moynihan of Chelsea
turns.text: I remember crossing into Gibraltar in 1964 when the border was threatened. You mentioned sovereignty. Will you be bound by EU rules on AI, product liability and cyber resilience? If so, do you look more like a British Overseas Territory or an EU one?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: Thank you for your long-standing interest. Our bond with the UK goes deeper than EU membership. What we've done is deal with reality: Gibraltar is physically attached to Europe, so people and goods need to flow. But this isn't free movement — we haven't given anyone the right to settle. On services, we're a free agent just like the UK. We can have the CPTPP, Japan, Morocco deals extended to us for services. We have little interest in goods trade — we're too small. We chose to compromise on things like genetically modified organisms, which we've never grown anyway, to keep growing in services.

turns.speaker: Lord Moynihan of Chelsea
turns.text: So you can't buy or research GM food from the UK, for example. That's a limitation.

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: We chose to make those compromises to keep growing in services. Since 2016, we haven't been able to bring in fresh produce that doesn't meet EU rules, but I hope the UK's reset with the EU will include an SPS agreement — food safety rules — so UK produce can come to Gibraltar. The UK may have to make similar compromises.

chapters.title: Closing Thanks
chapters.takeaway: The Chief Minister thanks the committee and announces he will be retiring soon.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you very much, Chief Minister. This has been most helpful, and I'm glad the video link worked. I'll close the public session.

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: May I say something before you close? Thank you and your committee, in all its configurations, for your interest in Gibraltar. I'll be retiring from office in the coming months, so this is likely my last appearance before you. Thank you for all your considerations over the past decade and a half.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We wish you a happy, productive and busy retirement. Thank you very much.
